title: Coimbatore's EssEmm Corporation Builds ₹100 Crore Business Automating Indian Kitchens
excerpt: Founded with ₹25,000 in 1997, the company's Cosmos-brand machines now cook curries, chapatis, and sweets in temples, hospitals, and restaurants across the globe.
body:
• EssEmm Corporation, founded by Satish Kumar Nair in Coimbatore in 1997, has grown from a ₹25,000 investment into a ₹100 crore kitchen automation company.
  • Its Cosmos-brand CookWok can stir, roast, and cook Indian curries with precision, serving ISKCON temples, hospitals, corporate cafeterias, and cloud kitchens.
  • The company has expanded to the US, UK, Middle East, Australia, and Singapore, with international certifications for its flagship products.
  • EssEmm manufactures 16 industrial kitchen appliances in-house and is investing heavily in R&D for further automation and food processing.

A Coimbatore-based kitchen equipment maker that started nearly three decades ago with ₹25,000 has quietly built itself into a ₹100 crore enterprise whose machines cook Indian food in temples, hospitals, and corporate cafeterias across the world.

EssEmm Corporation, founded in 1997 by Satish Kumar Nair, manufactures commercial kitchen equipment under the brand name Cosmos. Its product lineup includes robotic cooking woks, vegetable cutting machines, automatic chapati makers, wet grinders, and potato peelers — all designed to handle the specific demands of Indian cooking at scale.

From Workshop to Global Kitchen

Nair, a third-generation entrepreneur from a family with a long history of making kitchen equipment, established EssEmm to serve the booming hospitality and food catering sector. The company is headquartered on Sathy Road in Coimbatore's industrial district, a city long known as a manufacturing hub for engineering and industrial equipment.

The company's breakout product is the Cosmos CookWok, a robotic cooking system that can stir, roast, and cook Indian curries with precision. The machine handles the complex, multi-step process of preparing dishes like paneer tikka masala and even traditional South Indian sweets like Mysore pak — recipes that typically require skilled hands and constant attention.

"The cloud kitchen concept is disrupting the existing commercial kitchen space and provides a huge market opportunity, being the future of smart cooking."

— Satish Kumar Nair, Founder, EssEmm Corporation

In a recent feature by Curly Tales, journalist Kamiya Jani visited EssEmm's Coimbatore facility and put the CookWok to the test, preparing paneer tikka masala and Mysore pak using the automated system. The episode showcased vegetable cutting machines that chop kilos of produce in seconds and the CookWok's ability to replicate the consistency of a trained chef.

Serving Temples, Hospitals, and Cloud Kitchens

EssEmm's client base spans institutional and commercial kitchens. ISKCON temples in India and a Gurudwara in Sydney use the company's machines to prepare large-scale meals. Hospitals, corporate cafeterias, and the rapidly expanding cloud kitchen sector are also major buyers.

The company now manufactures 16 industrial kitchen appliances in-house under the Cosmos brand, including the upgraded CookWok Prime. Around 85 percent of its sales come from the domestic market, but EssEmm has been steadily building its export business, shipping products to the US, UK, Middle East, Australia, Europe, Africa, and Singapore.

EssEmm has obtained international certification for the US market for the CookWok Prime and is pursuing similar certifications across the European Union for its full product range. The company has also built partnerships with original equipment manufacturers in China and Taiwan to supplement its own manufacturing.

A Growing Market for Kitchen Automation

India's commercial kitchen equipment market has been expanding rapidly, driven by the growth of organised food service chains, cloud kitchens, and institutional catering. The shift toward automation has been accelerated by rising labor costs, hygiene concerns, and the need for consistency in large-scale food preparation.

Nair has said he sees particular potential in Indian cuisine-based restaurants overseas, where the complexity of dishes and the shortage of trained Indian chefs create a natural demand for automation.

"Equipments will help only on the texture. Skill of the chefs are still relevant. In a race, even though we have the best horse, the skill of the jockey is the most important factor."

— Satish Kumar Nair, in an interview with Kitchen Herald

Nair has consistently pushed back on the notion that machines will replace chefs, arguing that automation complements human skill rather than supplanting it. The company's focus is on handling repetitive, labour-intensive tasks — chopping, stirring, and temperature control — while leaving recipe design and quality judgement to trained professionals.

What This Means for the Diaspora

For Indian restaurants abroad, where finding and retaining skilled Indian chefs is a persistent challenge, commercial kitchen automation offers a practical solution. EssEmm's machines can replicate the consistency of traditional Indian cooking techniques, making it easier for diaspora entrepreneurs to scale restaurant operations without depending entirely on specialised labour.

Looking Ahead

EssEmm is investing in R&D for new product development and plans to expand into food processing and large-scale central kitchen concepts. The company is also building out its dish and ware washing solutions and specialty quick-service restaurant equipment.

From a small workshop in Coimbatore to kitchens on four continents, EssEmm's trajectory reflects a broader trend: Indian manufacturers are not just serving the domestic food industry but exporting the infrastructure of Indian cooking to the world.
